title: Start with a dictionary
goal: Read, access, and change named values in a Python dictionary.
prerequisites: You only need to recognize text, numbers, and the print function.

cells.title: What are the key and the value?
cells.explanation: A dictionary stores pairs: a key and its value. The key is a name you use to find a value, such as "Name" or "Age". Curly brackets create the dictionary; a colon separates each key from its value. Here, one dictionary describes one fictional student.
cells.code:
# Text uses quotes. A whole number does not need quotes.
student = {"Name": "Amira", "Age": 20, "Campus": "RAK"}
print(student)
print(type(student).__name__)
print(len(student))

questions.prompt: In "Age": 20, which part is the key and which part is the value?
questions.answer: "Age" is the key. The integer 20 is its value.

questions.prompt: What will len(student) print: the number of letters, pairs, or students?
questions.answer: It prints 3, the number of key-value pairs.
"20" is text; 20 is an integer. Numbers stored as text need conversion before arithmetic.

cells.task: Create a dictionary for Bilal, age 21, at Dubai. Add a fourth key called Program with value IT. Print the dictionary and its number of pairs.
cells.hint: Use four key: value pairs inside one pair of curly brackets.
cells.solution_note: The result has four pairs. Program is a new key, so the dictionary length increases to 4.

check.prompt: What does the colon do in "Age": 20?
options: It connects a key to its value.
It converts text to a number.
check.feedback: A colon separates a dictionary key from its associated value.

cells.solution_verify:
assert student['Name'] == 'Bilal' and student['Age'] == 21
assert student['Program'] == 'IT' and len(student) == 4
cells.watch: Do not mix up braces { } for dictionaries with brackets [ ] used for lists and access.
cells.takeaway: I can identify the keys, values, and number of pairs in a dictionary.

cells.title: Find a value by its key
cells.explanation: Square brackets after a dictionary look up a key. The key must match exactly, including upper and lower case. get() is useful when a key might be missing: you can supply a default value instead of raising KeyError.

questions.prompt: What does student["Name"] ask Python to find?
questions.answer: It asks for the value associated with the exact key "Name".

questions.prompt: What will the three print statements display?
questions.answer: Amira, then 20, then Not provided, each on a separate line.
No. The key is "Name", with an uppercase N. The different key "name" is absent, so direct access raises KeyError.

cells.task: Store the campus in campus. Use get() to request Program with the default "Undeclared" and save the value in program. Store whether "Age" is a key in has_age. Print all three values.
cells.hint: Use student["Campus"], student.get(...), and "Age" in student.
cells.solution:
student = {"Name": "Amira", "Age": 20, "Campus": "RAK"}
campus = student["Campus"]
program = student.get("Program", "Undeclared")
has_age = "Age" in student
print(campus)
print(program)
print(has_age)
cells.solution_note: Campus is RAK. Program is missing, so get() returns the chosen default. Membership with in checks keys, so has_age is True.

check.prompt: Which expression safely returns "Unknown" when Phone is missing?
check.feedback: get(key, default) supplies the default only when the requested key is absent.

cells.verify:
assert student['Name'] == 'Amira'
assert student.get('Email', 'Not provided') == 'Not provided'
cells.solution_verify: assert campus == 'RAK' and program == 'Undeclared' and has_age is True
cells.watch: A default from get() does not insert the missing key into the dictionary.
cells.takeaway: I can choose between direct key access and a safe lookup with a default.

cells.title: Change, add, and remove a pair
cells.explanation: Assigning a value to an existing key replaces its old value. Assigning to a new key adds a pair. pop() removes a key and returns its value. A dictionary cannot hold two separate entries with the same key.
cells.code:
student = {"Name": "Amira", "Age": 20, "Campus": "RAK"}
student["Age"] = 21
student["Program"] = "AI"
removed = student.pop("Campus")
print(student)
print("Removed:", removed)

questions.prompt: Which line changes an existing pair, and which line adds a new pair?
questions.answer: student["Age"] = 21 changes Age. student["Program"] = "AI" adds Program.

questions.prompt: How many pairs remain after Campus is removed?
Why does changing Age not increase the dictionary length?
questions.answer: Age already exists. Assignment replaces its value instead of adding a second Age key.

cells.task: Start with the same original dictionary. Increase Age by 2, add Program as IT, and remove Campus. Print the final dictionary.
cells.hint: Read the existing age on the right side of the assignment: student["Age"] + 2.
cells.solution:
student = {"Name": "Amira", "Age": 20, "Campus": "RAK"}
student["Age"] = student["Age"] + 2
student["Program"] = "IT"
student.pop("Campus")
print(student)
cells.solution_note: Age is 22 and Program is IT. Campus is no longer a key. Reading the old age lets the same calculation work for other starting ages.

check.prompt: What happens when you assign another value to an existing key?
options: A second identical key is added.
check.feedback: Each dictionary key identifies one entry; assigning to it replaces its associated value.

cells.watch: pop() raises KeyError for an absent key unless you also provide a default.
cells.takeaway: I can update a dictionary without confusing replacement with insertion.

cells.title: Read all keys and all pairs
cells.explanation: keys() gives the keys, values() gives their values, and items() gives key-value pairs. list() turns these views into lists that are easy to display. A for loop visits each pair in turn; the indented line runs once per pair.

questions.prompt: What two things are assigned to key and value on each loop turn?
questions.answer: One dictionary key and the value associated with that key.

questions.prompt: How many times does the indented print line run?
questions.answer: Three times, once for each pair.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between "RAK" in student and "RAK" in student.values()?
questions.answer: The first checks keys and is False. The second checks values and is True.

cells.task: Add Program as AI, print only the keys, and build a list named pairs using list(student.items()). Print pairs.
cells.hint: items() exposes both parts of each dictionary entry together.
cells.solution_note: There are four keys and four pairs. Each pair is displayed as a tuple, such as ("Program", "AI").

check.feedback: items() provides each key together with its value.

cells.watch: A Python dictionary preserves insertion order, but this does not mean the keys are alphabetically sorted.
cells.takeaway: I can inspect a dictionary and explain what a key-value loop does.
